summary.text:
Read on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 that went to Council on 23 February 2026 (cover paper 89272 with Appendices 1-4). Appendix 2 carries the prudential indicators - every table foots and every arithmetic identity ties.

The balance sheet identity holds exactly in every year of the six-year table. Total CFR £418.285m less external borrowing £288.528m less finance-lease liability £27.164m equals £102.593m internal borrowing at 31 March 2025 - matching Table 9 to the pound and the paper's own para 32 statement of '£102.6 million internal borrowing as at 1st April 2025'. Every year of the forecast identity closes without a rounding gap.

The loan-book aggregate ties to our file to the pound: 13 PWLB loans totalling £288,528,000, all MATURITY, all HRA, longest dated the 2071-03-28 loan at 1.88% for £20m. The paper states this at para 30 in words ('£288.5 million of external debt held at fixed rates with varying maturity terms up to 2071') and prints it in Table 9. Weighted rate is 3.77% on our side; the paper does not publish a weighted rate to test.

What the paper is actually about is the scale of the borrowing programme ahead. External debt is planned to rise from £288.5m at end of 2024/25 to £843.5m in 2029/30 - nearly tripling in five years, driven almost entirely by the HRA capital programme (£450.2m of new HRA prudential borrowing over 2026/27-29/30). The two-pool system means that HRA prudential borrowing must ultimately be externally funded. And the paper is very deliberate about not letting internal borrowing absorb the increment: under-borrowing goes from £102.6m to £128.6m over the plan while CFR goes 2.4x. Every incremental £1 of CFR is planned to hit the external market.

The HRA financing cost ratio is the striking indicator. Item 8 borrowing interest rises from £10.2m to £34.2m over the plan while the revenue stream rises from £58.3m to £84.4m; the ratio goes from -16.7% to -40.1%. That is a high number relative to the HRA outturn ratios we have read this year. The paper defends it with the interest cover ratio graph (target 1.25:1, holds through 50 years) and by anchoring to the 40-year HRA business plan. Not a distress signal - the numbers are consistent - but a very deliberate leverage decision.

The interest-rate forecast used is MUFG's from 22 December 2025 - Bank Rate expected to fall from 3.75% to 3.25% by end 2026, 10y PWLB drifting from 5.20% to 4.70% over the plan. Eight months on, Bank Rate has been held (not cut) and long rates have drifted higher rather than lower. The interest-payable line (£18.2m rising to £33.4m) was priced against the December central case; today's curve gives essentially the same short end and slightly higher long end.

Officer address situation: cover paper names 'Group Finance Director' (S151) as the report source without a name; Cabinet Member is Councillor Ed Turner. The report author, Bill Lewis (Financial Accounting Manager), has a published email (blewis@oxford.gov.uk). Bill is not the S151 - address to him with a request to forward to the Group Finance Director rather than presuming.

officer.body:
Hi Bill,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet. If the Group Finance Director is the right addressee I'd be grateful if you'd forward - the paper doesn't name them so I'm writing to you as the report author.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more - the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief - in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 that went to Council on 23 February, ahead of the next treasury cycle. You're not being singled out - every authority gets one of these - and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is clearly laid out and the arithmetic across Appendix 2 foots to the pound, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The reason we wrote is that the loan book you describe at cover paragraph 30 sits in our file exactly. Thirteen PWLB loans totalling £288,528,000, all fixed-rate maturity loans, all HRA, running out to 2071 - the longest is a £20m maturity at 1.88% due 28 March 2071. That is what your paragraph says in words and what your Appendix 2 Table 9 prints at £288,528k. The reconciliation ties to the pound. It doesn't happen every time we read a paper - it costs one sentence and it settles the question of whether to keep reading.

What the numbers around it show us is worth naming. Your Table 9 puts external debt at £843.5m by 2029/30 - nearly tripling from £288.5m in five years. Alongside it, the Under-Borrowing line runs 102.6, 114.2, 128.3, 128.0, 128.6, 128.6. So the internal-borrowing figure widens by only £26m across the plan while your CFR goes from £418m to £999m. Every incremental pound of CFR is planned to hit the external market. Table 8 shows why - Total Core Funds are flat at around £168m from 2026/27 onwards and Working Capital is held at -£25.7m throughout. There is no headroom in reserves for a larger internal-borrowing bridge. That is a very deliberate leverage decision, and one we don't see stated as plainly in most strategies we read.

The HRA financing-cost ratio at your Table 6 is the second thing worth naming. Item 8 borrowing interest goes from £10.2m to £34.2m across the plan against a revenue stream that goes from £58.3m to £84.4m, and the ratio moves from -16.7% (2024/25 actual) to -40.1% (2029/30). The 40% number is towards the top end of what we've read this year. The 1.25:1 interest cover ratio graph and the 40-year HRA business plan are the load-bearing pieces of evidence that this is affordable, and the chart shows the ICR closest to the 1.25 line around 2027/28. Nothing follows from us as advice - we don't sell treasury products and only your business plan and adviser can validate the affordability envelope - but the shape of the number is unusual enough to note.

One page you might find useful: the per-loan valuation of your PWLB book against the DMO's premature repayment curve is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, updated daily. Your paper doesn't discuss rescheduling, and it's not for us to raise it as a course of action, but the sub-3% loans at the long end of your book (the £20m 2071 at 1.88%, the £38.5m 2057 at 3.50%, the £40m 2042 at 3.50%) sit at deep indicative discounts on our curve today. Indicative only - the DMO is the only binding quote and we model no MRP or accounting treatment. Just visible on the page daily.

The forecast in your Table 1 is worth an eye. MUFG's 22 December central case had Bank Rate falling to 3.50% by June and 3.25% by December this year, and 10-year PWLB drifting from 5.20% to 4.70% over the plan. On the 14 August fixing Bank Rate is still 3.75% - no cut in the eight months since MUFG published - and the long end has drifted higher rather than lower. Your interest-payable line at paragraph 57 (£18.2m rising to £33.4m) was priced against the December central case; today's curve gives essentially the same short end and slightly higher long. Not a hedge recommendation from us - just what the pricing looks like against the December view your strategy was built on.

And for the market you would be borrowing into if you draw the £555m of net new external borrowing your Table 9 projects across the plan, the monthly PWLB activity for the sector - split by HRA and General Fund, by council and by tenor - is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. There's rarely a peer group of councils with a £450m HRA borrowing programme ahead of them, and the shape of what neighbours have done recently is the closest reference point we can offer.

On training, four fit. Reading the PWLBpredict and SONIA Forward Curve & OIS speak to your economic section (paragraphs 9-10, and Tables 1-2 showing the 'Now vs Previously' downward revision to earnings rates). The HRA business plan and treasury pairs with your Table 6 ratio work and the interest-cover-ratio chart at paragraph 11. And Liability benchmark modelling for treasury goes to the three LB charts in Appendix 2 - the all-Council chart on p. 371, the GF chart on p. 372 and the HRA chart on p. 373, all of which show the CFR line moving well above your current debt profile through the late 2020s. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 - Council 23 February 2026, cover paper (agenda item 13, pp. 337-349) and Appendices 1-4 (pp. 351-377) at mycouncil.oxford.gov.uk.
